issues.legal_issue: The acquittal of some accused does not defeat liability based on membership in an unlawful assembly when reliable findings establish that at least five people participated.
material_facts: The appellant arrived with four companions to prevent the erection of a fence, and the court found that the group shared an unlawful object.
Three of the five accused were acquitted, but the court concluded that the acquittals did not alter the finding that the appellant and at least four others formed the assembly.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal of three accused did not negate the unlawful assembly or prevent the appellant’s conviction on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 141 and 149 of the IPC, an assembly is unlawful when five or more persons share an object specified in Section 141. The number of persons ultimately convicted need not itself be five if the evidence establishes that other persons participated in the assembly. The Court relied on Khem Karan v. State of U.P. and Dharam Pal v. State of U.P.

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_proceeding and participants_numbered_five_or_more and appellant_shared_unlawful_object and some_participants_were_acquitted_or_not_convicted

predicates.unlawful_assembly_proceeding: The case concerns criminal liability based on participation in an alleged unlawful assembly.
predicates.participants_numbered_five_or_more: The court found that at least five people participated in the assembly, including any participants who were not convicted.
predicates.appellant_shared_unlawful_object: The appellant shared the assembly’s unlawful object.
predicates.some_participants_were_acquitted_or_not_: Some alleged participants were acquitted or were not convicted.

issues.definition: When an unlawful-assembly case establishes at least five participants and the appellant shared the unlawful object, acquittals or non-convictions of some participants do not prevent liability for membership in the assembly.

issues.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly is not liable for a murder committed by another member unless the murder was committed to advance the assembly’s common object or the member knew it was likely to be committed in advancing that object.
material_facts: The group came to prevent the erection of a fence, not to kill the deceased.
The appellant was unarmed and used only his hands to push, slap, and box people at the scene.
The fatal stabbing was carried out by another group member, and the evidence did not establish that the appellant knew that member carried a knife.
Other alleged weapons were not used, and the deceased was being helped away after receiving a blow when he was stabbed.
issues.conclusion: The appellant’s conviction for murder with the aid of Section 149 IPC was unsustainable, and he was acquitted of that charge.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 IPC applies if an offence is committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object, or if members knew that the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. Whether such knowledge existed is inferred from the totality of the circumstances, including the assembly’s nature, weapons, and conduct. The Court relied on Lalji v. State of U.P.; Dharam Pal v. State of U.P.; Chikkarange Gowda v. State of Mysore; Gajanand v. State of U.P., approving Ram Charan Rai v. Emperor; Mizaji v. State of U.P.; Shambhu Nath Singh v. State of Bihar; Gangadhar Behera v. State of Orissa; and Bishna alias Bhiswadeb Mahato v. State of West Bengal.

rule.if: appeal_from_murder_conviction_via_group_liability and common_object_was_nonlethal_interference and appellant_was_unarmed and no_evidence_appellant_knew_deadly_weapon_was_present and fatal_weapon_was_not_used_to_advance_common_object

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction_via_group_: The proceeding challenges a murder conviction imposed on the basis of the accused’s membership in a group.
predicates.common_object_was_nonlethal_interference: The group’s common object was to interfere with or prevent conduct, rather than to kill or inflict fatal injury.
predicates.appellant_was_unarmed: The appellant carried no weapon and used only unarmed force.
predicates.no_evidence_appellant_knew_deadly_weapon: The evidence did not show that the appellant knew a group member carried a weapon capable of causing death.
predicates.fatal_weapon_was_not_used_to_advance_com: The fatal weapon was used in a sudden act that the court found was not in prosecution of the group’s common object.

issues.definition: Where a murder appeal based on group liability involves a nonlethal common object, an unarmed appellant, no evidence of knowledge of a deadly weapon, and a fatal act outside that object, murder liability through group membership is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A court may reduce a sentence for bodily-injury offences and order compensation when the circumstances justify that sentencing outcome.
material_facts: The appellant’s convictions for bodily-injury offences were upheld, including an offence involving a fracture.
He had faced a prolonged trial and appeal, had no criminal antecedents, and had already served part of his sentence.
He offered to compensate the victims and was able to pay; the court considered the injuries and the victims’ losses.
issues.conclusion: The Court reduced the custodial sentence for the offence involving the fracture to the period already served and ordered compensation for the victims, with the original sentence to revive if the required deposit was not made.
issues.legal_principle: Section 357 of the CrPC empowers a court to award compensation to victims, including in addition to other sentences. The amount and use of that power depend on the circumstances, including the nature of the offence and injury, the victim’s claim and needs, and the offender’s ability to pay. The Court relied on Hansa v. State of Punjab, Hari Singh v. Sukhbir Singh, Manish Jalan v. State of Karnataka, and Rachpal Singh v. State of Punjab, and referred to the Law Commission’s 42nd Report.

rule.if: appeal_from_bodily_injury_conviction and prolonged_proceedings and no_prior_criminal_record and part_of_sentence_already_served and offender_offered_compensation_and_could_pay

predicates.appeal_from_bodily_injury_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by a person convicted of an offence causing bodily injury.
predicates.prolonged_proceedings: The offender experienced a prolonged trial or appellate process.
predicates.no_prior_criminal_record: The offender had no prior criminal history.
predicates.part_of_sentence_already_served: The offender had already served part of the custodial sentence.
predicates.offender_offered_compensation_and_could_: The offender offered compensation and the court found the offender able to pay it.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a bodily-injury conviction, prolonged proceedings, no prior criminal record, time already served, and an offer of affordable compensation may support reducing custody and ordering compensation.
